title: Maximum Score of a Good Subarray
statement:
You get an integer array `nums` (0-indexed) and an index `k`. For a contiguous subarray covering indices `i` through `j`, its **score** is the smallest value among `nums[i..j]` multiplied by its length `j - i + 1`. A subarray is **good** when it includes index `k`, that is, `i <= k <= j`.

Return the largest score that any good subarray can have.
notes:
## Intuition

Every good subarray is a window that grows outward from index `k`. Checking all pairs `(i, j)` with `i <= k <= j` is O(n²) or worse. Instead, grow one window greedily from `[k, k]`, one element at a time, always taking the **larger** of the two neighbours. Taking the larger neighbour keeps the window's minimum as high as possible for as long as possible, so for every minimum value the window passes through, it is as wide as it can be while keeping that minimum. The best answer has some minimum `m`, and its widest window with all values at least `m` is one of the windows we visit.

## Approach

1. Start with `left = right = k`, `minimum = nums[k]` and `best = nums[k]`.
2. While the window can still grow on some side, read `leftValue` and `rightValue`, the neighbours just outside it, using 0 for a side that has hit the array's edge (all values are at least 1, so that side is never chosen).
3. If `leftValue < rightValue`, extend `right`; otherwise extend `left`. Update `minimum` with the new element.
4. Score the window as `minimum * (right - left + 1)` and keep the largest in `best`.
5. Return `best` once the window covers the whole array.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 4, 3, 7, 4, 5]`, `k = 3`: start with window `[7]`, `best = 7`. Neighbours 3 and 4: take 4, minimum 4, score `4 * 2 = 8`. Neighbours 3 and 5: take 5, score `4 * 3 = 12`. The right edge is reached, so take 3: minimum 3, score `3 * 4 = 12`. Take 4: score `3 * 5 = 15`. Take 1: score `1 * 6 = 6`. The answer is `15`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n), the window grows by one element per step.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- When one side reaches the array's edge the loop must keep extending the other side; the 0 sentinel handles that without extra branches.
- On equal neighbours either choice works: whichever one is taken first, the other is taken before the minimum can fall below their value.
- The window must always contain `k`; trying ordinary "largest rectangle" windows that skip `k` gives too big an answer.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `left`, `right` | the current window's ends; it always contains `k` |
| `minimum` | the smallest value inside the window |
| `best` | the highest score seen so far |
| `leftValue`, `rightValue` | the values just outside each end (0 past the edge) |

narration.2: The window starts as just index k, so it is good from the beginning.
narration.4: A one-element window has that element as its minimum.
narration.5: Its score, nums[k] times 1, is the first candidate answer.
narration.7: Keep growing while at least one side can still extend.
narration.8: The value just left of the window, or 0 when the left edge is reached.
narration.9: The value just right of the window, or 0 when the right edge is reached.
narration.10: Grow toward the larger neighbour so the minimum drops as slowly as possible.
narration.11: Extend the window one step to the right.
narration.12: The new element may lower the window's minimum.
narration.14: Otherwise extend the window one step to the left.
narration.15: Again the new element may lower the minimum.
narration.17: Score the grown window and keep the best score.
narration.19: Every width has been tried with its best minimum; return the top score.
